description: 5 HARD-level code questions on Python Variables (Part 2 of 2). Tuple swap, cross-type rebinding, del/NameError, function-local vs global scope, and assigning to keywords. Computed outputs verified with Python 3.

questions.question:
What does this code print?

a, b = 10, 20
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)
questions.answer:
OUTPUT:
20 10

EXPLANATION:
The right-hand side (b, a) is fully evaluated to (20, 10) BEFORE the unpacking assignment writes anything. Then a gets 20 and b gets 10 - no temporary variable needed. This is the idiomatic Python swap.

code:
a, b = 10, 20
a, b = b, a    # reads (20, 10), then writes a=20, b=10
print(a, b)    # 20 10

WHY IT MATTERS:
In C/Java you need a temp: tmp = a; a = b; b = tmp. In Python the tuple constructor + unpacking does it atomically in one statement. The same mechanism powers rotations: a, b, c = b, c, a - handy in circular buffer and state-machine code.

questions.question:
What does this code print?

data = [1, 2, 3]
data = "text"
data = 9.5
print(type(data).__name__)
questions.answer:
OUTPUT:
float

EXPLANATION:
The same name data is rebound to a list, then a string, then a float. Python tracks the TYPE OF THE OBJECT, not the name. After data = 9.5, the name points at a float, so type(data).__name__ returns the string "float".

code:
data = [1, 2, 3]   # data -> list
data = "text"      # data -> str (rebinding, not conversion)
data = 9.5         # data -> float
print(type(data).__name__)  # float

WHY IT MATTERS:
Rebinding is NOT converting: the old objects are simply discarded (garbage-collected). This is different from int(data), which CREATES a new object and leaves the original untouched. Reusing names across types is legal but hurts readability - type hints (@dataclass, mypy) exist partly to keep yourself honest here.

questions.question:
What happens when this code runs?

x = 100
del x
print(x)
questions.answer:
OUTPUT:
NameError: name 'x' is not defined

EXPLANATION:
del x unbinds the name x from its object (the object itself may survive if other references exist). After that, any use of x fails because no such name exists in the current scope - so print(x) raises NameError.

code:
x = 100
del x        # remove the binding, not necessarily the object
print(x)     # NameError: name 'x' is not defined

WHY IT MATTERS:
del is not just for variables:
del lst[0]       # remove list item by INDEX
lst.remove(v)    # remove by VALUE (different!)
del d["key"]     # remove a dict key
del obj.attr     # remove an attribute
Using a variable you deleted is a classic NameError; catch it by checking the name still exists or restructuring code so deletion is avoidable (e.g. just rebind instead).

questions.question:
What does this code print?

count = 10

def update():
    count = 99
    return count

update()
print(count)
questions.answer:
OUTPUT:
10

EXPLANATION:
Inside update(), the line count = 99 CREATES a new local variable - it does not touch the global count. Python decides a name is local to a function if it is assigned anywhere in that function (unless declared global/nonlocal). The returned 99 is discarded because the call update() is not assigned to anything, so the module-level count stays 10.

code:
count = 10            # module-level (global) variable

def update():
    count = 99        # NEW local count - shadows the global
    return count

update()              # return value 99 is thrown away
print(count)          # 10 - the global was never modified

WHY IT MATTERS:
To really modify the global you need: global count at the top of the function - or, much better, return the new value and assign it: count = update(). The local-shadowing rule is why a function can't "accidentally" clobber globals, and also why using a global without global inside a function raises UnboundLocalError.

questions.question:
What happens when this code runs?

True = 5
questions.answer:
OUTPUT:
SyntaxError: cannot assign to True

EXPLANATION:
True (and False, None) are reserved keywords in Python, not variables - assigning to them is illegal and the error is raised at PARSE time, before any code executes. The same happens for all keywords: if, for, class, def, import, while, return, etc.

code:
True = 5   # SyntaxError: cannot assign to True
if = 10    # SyntaxError: invalid syntax

WHY IT MATTERS:
Because True/False/None are keywords, you can never shadow them (good). But note: True == 1 is True, so if someone accidentally redefines the name true (not True), Python happily creates a variable named true. Watch typo'd keywords and case variants - they silently become valid identifiers instead of errors.
